headline: DHS appears to axe plan to construct immigration detention megacenter in small Georgia town
summary: ICE abandoned plans for a 10,000-bed detention center in Social Circle, GA due to local resistance and infrastructure concerns. This reversal comes after months of tension between the city and federal government, and follows a lawsuit filed by Social Circle against DHS and ICE. The project gained national attention due to its location in a deep-red county, with 70% voting for Trump in '24.

headline: Two health departments will offer preventative Lyme disease treatment due to ‘extreme tick season’
summary: Two West Virginia health departments offer medication to prevent Lyme disease if taken within 72 hours of a tick bite. Cases have quadrupled since 2020, prompting this public health measure. The state also tracks alpha-gal syndrome, a rising tick-borne meat allergy.

headline: Budget committee hears update on ICE detention cost, electrical grid analysis grant
summary: Indiana's Department of Correction is operating at a profit from its immigration detention contract, expecting detainee numbers to increase. The state receives approximately $291 per bed per day from ICE.

headline: Virginia budget leaders reach ‘agreement in principle’ for deal, more state headlines
summary: The Virginia Mercury reports that state budget leaders have reached an 'agreement in principle' for a deal.

headline: NC Senate passes expansive revenue bill changing vape enforcement, R&D tax breaks
summary: The North Carolina Senate passed a revenue bill (SB 595), which includes financial exploitation protections and hurricane relief provisions. Democrats opposed it due to changes in research & development tax deductions, but Republicans emphasized the bill's broader importance. The House will now vote on this bill.

headline: NM U.S. Reps. Vasquez, Leger Fernández introduce New World screwworm legislation
summary: New Mexico's first New World screwworm case has led to bipartisan legislation, the Protecting America’s Herds Act, aimed at curbing its spread. The bill, introduced by U.S. Representatives Gabe Vasquez and Teresa Leger Fernández, seeks to fund cooperative extension services for training in identification, treatment, and prevention of the parasitic fly that affects livestock and pets. Critics argue that the USDA's response has been insufficient, with a delayed sterile-fly production facility in Texas. The legislation is backed by several agricultural associations and aims to prioritize funding for high-risk areas.

headline: New Mexico Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver suspends Dem Lt. Gov. campaign, citing health
summary: Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver suspends her campaign for lieutenant governor due to health concerns, triggering a selection process by the Democratic Party's State Central Committee.

headline: ICE plans to offload Berks County and Schuylkill County warehouses, report says
summary: The Department of Homeland Security plans to sell two Pennsylvania warehouses it purchased for potential immigration detention centers due to infrastructure limitations and local opposition.

headline: ICE scraps plans for Romulus detention center, AG says
summary: ICE abandoned plans for a detention center in Romulus due to local opposition, environmental concerns, and legal challenges led by Michigan's Attorney General.

headline: Finger-pointing abounds from Michigan House, Senate leaders as July 1 budget deadline looms
summary: As Michigan lawmakers near the July 1 budget deadline, negotiations have slowed due to disagreements over a Republican property tax reform proposal. House Speaker Matt Hall suggested missing both deadlines and using a continuing resolution, while Democrats insist on meeting the statutory target. Schools could face budget planning challenges if a deal is not reached by July 1.

headline: State police seeking ICE raid protester, even as earlier arrests yielded no charges
summary: Vermont State Police continue investigating March's ICE raid protests despite Chittenden County State’s Attorney declining to charge arrested protesters.

headline: UVM Health is downsizing. Here’s what those cuts mean for services.
summary: In Vermont, UVM Health Network's layoff of over 140 employees, primarily support staff and directors, aims to save $9.5 million annually towards a goal of cutting expenses by $300 million in three years; concerns raised about potential impacts on patient care quality and wait times due to reduced staffing.

headline: Salah Sarsour released from ICE detention after pressure from family, supporters, elected officials
summary: A federal judge ordered the release of Salah Sarsour, a Muslim leader arrested by immigration agents over his political speech supporting Palestinian rights. The decision came after sustained pressure from family, community, and officials. The ruling finds potential First Amendment retaliation but has no bearing on his ongoing deportation proceedings.

headline: Affordability tax credit likely not available for Colorado families in next two years
summary: The Family Affordability Tax Credit for low-income families may not activate for the next two years due to insufficient revenue growth, affecting child poverty rates. Colorado's budget faces future challenges despite recent cuts and projected modest surpluses over TABOR caps. H.R.1 impacts are expected to reduce corporate income tax collections but increase individual income tax revenues. The state predicts a 40% chance of an economic recession in the coming year.

headline: ICE plans to offload Salt Lake City warehouse, report says
summary: The federal government's purchase of a Salt Lake City warehouse for use as an ICE detention facility is under review, with DHS reportedly considering selling it. Local leaders sue to halt its conversion, citing overburdened infrastructure and inhumane conditions. The planned sale could impact immigration enforcement capacity in Utah.

headline: Gov. Landry sued over plan to move public school funding to teacher stipends
summary: Three advocates sued Louisiana officials over Gov. Landry's plan to cut K-12 school operations funds for teacher pay stipends, claiming it violates state constitution and circumvents legislative process.

headline: Regents vote to increase NU tuition by 4.25%, cut $8 million in next $1.19 billion budget
summary: The University of Nebraska Board of Regents approved a $1.19 billion operating budget for 2025-26, including a 4.25% tuition increase to mitigate future budget cuts and fund non-union faculty/staff pay increases. The budget also calls for $8 million in cuts through operational efficiency. State funding only increased by 0.62%, falling short of NU's requested 3.5% inflation-based increase. Regents expressed concern about affordability and the impact of ongoing budget cuts on students and programs.

headline: 2 more cruise ship passengers leave Omaha quarantine after deadly hantavirus outbreak
summary: UNMC's National Quarantine Unit housed passengers from a cruise ship affected by hantavirus. After five weeks of monitoring, two more passengers returned home early but were advised to self-monitor for up to 42 days due to delayed symptom onset. Six passengers remain in quarantine until May 31. This incident highlights Nebraska's role as a regional hub for managing infectious diseases and the importance of coordinated public health efforts with federal agencies and other states.

headline: Greenwood Leflore Hospital warns of closure as Medicaid moves to withhold $2.4 million payment
summary: Mississippi's Division of Medicaid seeks to withhold a $2.4 million payment from Greenwood Leflore Hospital due to outstanding debts, which could force the struggling facility to close by June 30. This could impact public health in the region by limiting access to healthcare services for residents. The hospital has asked a judge to order the payment or face closure, arguing that without it, they cannot finalize an agreement with UMMC for takeover and maintain operations. The transfer of the hospital's operations to UMMC is seen as the only viable option to continue providing quality healthcare in Leflore County and surrounding areas.

headline: Labor and faith groups decry federal indictment of 15 anti-ICE protesters
summary: Tens of thousands protested ICE presence in Minneapolis; 15 protesters charged, sparking condemnation from labor and religious groups who accuse Trump admin of political repression. Human Rights Watch report details abuses during Operation Metro Surge, urging accountability for federal agents.

headline: Polling shows Midwestern voters concerned about home insurance cost
summary: Midwestern homeowners' concerns about rising insurance premiums are high (75%), with 86% wanting officials to act. They favor policies holding utilities and polluters accountable, with broad support for insurer disclosure, cooperation with local officials, disaster resistance funding, and recovering funds from polluters.

headline: Los republicanos de Kansas podrían intentar retrasar la elección al Senado si Marshall deja el cargo
summary: Kansas senatorial election controversy: Republican Senator Roger Marshall might resign for Trump administration post, potentially delaying his seat's election until 2028 due to a new law requiring gubernatorial appointments from a legislatively approved list. This could impact democratic representation and spark political unrest among voters awaiting their voting rights.

headline: CT tried to control hospital fees. Patients still feel blindsided, wary of seeking care
summary: The article discusses the growing trend of hospital facility fees charged to patients, even for routine outpatient treatment, with Connecticut reporting over $2 billion in such fees in 2024. These fees can cause confusion and financial burden on patients, with advocates criticizing them as a tool for private equity firms to extract profits. Despite attempts by lawmakers to curtail these fees, hospitals argue they are necessary for operational expenses. The state has regulations on facility fees but lacks robust enforcement mechanisms due to limitations in data collection and few patient complaints.

headline: State workers fight Newsom’s return-to-office mandate
summary: California state workers protested Gov. Gavin Newsom's mandate for them to return to offices four days a week, with dozens appearing at a Senate hearing to support a bill that would strengthen telework standards and provide more flexibility.
